428.title: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 90)
428.word: Teach us to number our days
428.hook: a thousand years are like yesterday; teach us to count our days
428.howItsDone: Psalm 90 is often read at Christian funerals and on New Year's Eve, and Isaac Watts's hymn based on it, "O God, Our Help in Ages Past," is sung at memorials and remembrance services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sparrow nesting by the altar. Your line was even the sparrow has a home. Who or what did you make room for? Day four hundred twenty-eight.

Some people keep a jar of marbles on a shelf. One marble for every Saturday they might reasonably have left, worked out from their age. Every Saturday morning, they take one out and drop it in a bowl. It sounds grim. The people who do it usually say the opposite: the shrinking jar makes the Saturdays better. They stop wasting them. That idea is very old. There is exactly one psalm whose heading carries the name of Moses, and it's about this: the shortness of a life held against the length of God. Today, Psalm ninety, and a request to learn how to count.
screen: `A JAR OF MARBLES.` → `ONE FOR EACH SATURDAY LEFT.` → `MOSES' ONLY PSALM.`

segments.voice: The heading reads, "A Prayer of Moses the man of God." It's the only psalm with his name on it, and it opens the fourth of the five books of the Psalms. It starts with God's size: "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations." Before the mountains were born, you were God. Then it zooms out until time itself shrinks: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night." A watch was a few hours of guard duty. A thousand years, gone like a night shift. Next to that, human life looks like grass, the psalm says, green in the morning and cut down by evening. It even gives a number: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten." Seventy. Eighty, if strong. "For it is soon cut off, and we fly away." This could have ended in gloom. Instead it turns into a request. "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." To number is to count, the way you'd count coins. The same root shows up in the writing on the wall in the book of Daniel: mene, numbered. The psalm doesn't ask to be spared the counting. It asks to be taught to count well, so that the counting turns into wisdom instead of fear. And the last verse asks for something lasting: "establish thou the work of our hands." Isaac Watts turned this psalm into a hymn in 1719, O God, Our Help in Ages Past, and it's still sung at funerals and on national days of mourning.
screen: `A THOUSAND YEARS LIKE YESTERDAY` · `THREESCORE YEARS AND TEN` · `TEACH US TO COUNT, NOT TO FEAR` · `ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS` · then, large: `SO TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count the days left in this month. Work it out now, on your fingers if you like. Hold the number. It's smaller than it feels, isn't it? Now, for the sit, let a few of those days come to mind one at a time. Not as a to-do list. Just ask of each one: what would make this day worth keeping? A call, a walk, a meal with someone, an apology. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: so teach us to number our days. If you don't, just hold the number gently, without panic. The bell holds the time.
Teach us to number our days. Moses' prayer in Psalm ninety: count your days, so that counting turns into wisdom.
screen: `TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: number our days. Tonight, before sleep, count one thing today held that you'd want to keep. Just one. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

429.title: Under his wings (Psalm 91)
429.hook: he shall cover you with his feathers
429.howItsDone: Psalm 91 is a night psalm for many Christians: it is prayed at Compline in Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran traditions, and many people pray it for protection before travel, surgery or military service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' prayer and a life worth counting. Your line was number our days. What was the one thing from yesterday you'd want to keep? Day four hundred twenty-nine.

A shadow crosses the farmyard. A hawk, circling low. The hen doesn't run. She makes one sharp sound, and every chick within earshot comes skittering across the dirt and disappears under her. In two seconds there's no chick to be seen, only a hen who suddenly looks twice her size, feathers puffed, eyes on the sky. Underneath, it's warm and dark and loud with heartbeats. Anyone who has kept chickens has seen it. The writers of the Bible had seen it too, and they used it for God. Today, Psalm ninety-one, a psalm many people say at night, and the picture of being hidden under wings.
screen: `A HAWK'S SHADOW.` → `THE HEN CALLS.` → `NO CHICKS IN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty." Then, verse four: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust." The Hebrew word for wing is kanaf. It also means the edge of a cloak. In the book of Ruth, Boaz blesses Ruth, the foreigner who has come to Israel, as one who has come to trust under the wings of the God of Israel. Later, at night, Ruth asks Boaz to spread his kanaf, his cloak, over her, and the King James Bible translates it skirt. Wings and a cloak: both are ways of saying you're covered, you belong. The psalm goes on: "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day." Which is why so many people pray it at bedtime. Jews say it in their night prayers, and many churches pray it at Compline, the last service of the day. But there's a twist. In the Gospels, when the devil tempts Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple, he quotes this very psalm: he shall give his angels charge over thee. Go on, jump. And Jesus answers, "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." The psalm is a place to hide, not a dare to take. And Jesus used the same farmyard picture himself, over Jerusalem: how often would I have gathered thy children together, "even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."
screen: `COVERED WITH HIS FEATHERS` · `KANAF: A WING, A CLOAK'S EDGE` · `NO TERROR BY NIGHT` · `A SHELTER, NOT A DARE` · then, large: `UNDER HIS WINGS SHALT THOU TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for protection for someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who could use covering right now. Someone traveling, someone sick, someone scared, a kid walking into a hard week. Picture them clearly: where they are, what they're facing. If you pray, you can ask God to cover them with his feathers, in the psalm's own words, or simply say their name to God and leave it there. If you don't pray, hold them in mind and wish them safe, steadily, the way a hen sits still. The bell holds the time.
Under his wings. Psalm ninety-one's picture of God as a bird sheltering its young, said by many at night.
Your line: under his wings. Tonight, as the lights go off, name one person you'd want sheltered, and keep them in mind as you fall asleep. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

430.title: Sing a new song (Psalm 96)
430.hook: let the fields be joyful and the trees sing
430.tomorrow: bless the Lord, O my soul
430.howItsDone: Psalm 96 is sung in many churches at Christmas and other feasts, and Christians often take its call to "sing a new song" as a reason to write new hymns and worship music for each generation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hen gathering her chicks, and a psalm said at night. Your line was under his wings. Who did you keep in mind as the lights went off? Day four hundred thirty.

When did you last sing something for the first time? Not the chorus stuck in your head since the drive to work. Not the birthday song, or the anthem before the game, or the hymn you could sing in your sleep. Something new in your own mouth. For most adults, it's been years. We hum what we already know. There's comfort in that, and nothing wrong with it. But the Psalms keep asking for something else. Again and again they say: sing a new song. And Psalm ninety-six doesn't stop at people. By the end, the fields, the sea and the trees are singing too.
screen: `THE SAME CHORUS, AGAIN.` → `WHEN DID YOU LAST SING SOMETHING NEW?` → `EVEN THE TREES JOIN IN.`

segments.voice: Psalm ninety-six opens, in the King James Bible: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth." That phrase, a new song, turns up in several psalms, in the prophet Isaiah, and then twice in Revelation, the Bible's last book, where it's still being called new. So new here doesn't mean the latest hit. In the Psalms, a new song usually answers something new God has done: a rescue, a victory, a homecoming. Fresh mercy deserves fresh words. And this new song isn't for one nation. All the earth. The psalm tells the families of the peoples to give glory, and it says the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens. Then the song spreads beyond people altogether. "Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof. Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice." Why are the trees so happy? The last verse says: "For he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth." That sounds alarming, but listen to how it ends: "he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth." In the Psalms, judgment often means setting things right. Crooked made straight. The trees cheer because justice is finally coming. And this psalm has a second home. Most of it appears again in First Chronicles, as part of the song sung when David brought the ark of the covenant into Jerusalem. A new song, sung on a day of arrival.
screen: `NEW SONG, FROM PSALMS TO REVELATION` · `FRESH MERCY, FRESH WORDS` · `THE FIELDS AND TREES REJOICE` · `JUDGMENT: THINGS SET RIGHT` · then, large: `O SING UNTO THE LORD A NEW SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing something new. Nobody's listening, or if they are, that's their luck. Take the psalm's first line, O sing unto the Lord a new song, and give it a tune that didn't exist a minute ago. Hum it first. Then try the words. It can be three notes. It can be off key. If you'd rather, sing a hymn or a song you've never sung aloud before. If you pray, let it be your prayer. If you don't, let it be a small act of courage. Then rest in the quiet after. The bell holds the time.
Sing a new song. Psalm ninety-six's call to all the earth: fresh words for fresh mercy, with the fields and trees joining in.
Your line: a new song. Today, try one new thing with your voice. Sing in the shower, hum a tune you just made up, or read a psalm aloud for the first time. Day four hundred thirty.

431.title: Bless the Lord, O my soul (Psalm 103)
431.hook: he knows our frame; he remembers we are dust
431.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 103 as a prayer of thanksgiving, and it is sung in hymns such as Henry Francis Lyte's "Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven."

segments.voice: Yesterday, fields and trees joining the singing. Your line was a new song. Did your voice try something it had never done? Day four hundred thirty-one.

Memory is strangely lopsided. A teacher's sharp comment in seventh grade: still there, word for word, decades later. The stranger who held a door when your arms were full of groceries last Tuesday: gone by Wednesday. We keep the wounds on file and let the kindnesses slip through. It isn't a moral failing exactly. Minds seem to be built to watch for threats. But it means that, left alone, most of us remember our lives as harder and lonelier than they were. Psalm one hundred three knows this. It opens with a person giving their own soul a firm reminder, almost a nudge in the ribs. Don't forget.
screen: `THE SHARP COMMENT: KEPT.` → `THE HELD DOOR: FORGOTTEN.` → `A NUDGE TO YOUR OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred three begins, in the King James Bible: "Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." Like the deer psalm, the writer is talking to himself. But this time it isn't comfort. It's a reminder. Don't forget. Then he counts the benefits out loud, one after another: who forgives, who heals, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with lovingkindness, who renews your youth like the eagle's. Notice something about this psalm. It doesn't ask for anything. No request, no complaint, from beginning to end. It just remembers. Then come some of the tenderest lines in the Bible. "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." East and west never meet; you can travel east forever. "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust." Frame is how we're put together, what we're made of. God knows we're breakable, the psalm says, and is gentle about it. Our days are like grass, the wind passes over, and the place forgets us. And then the turn: "But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting." We forget. God remembers that we're dust, and remembers mercy. By the end the psalm calls on the angels, every work of God, and finally its own soul again. Henry Francis Lyte turned it into a hymn in 1834, Praise, My Soul, the King of Heaven, and many churches still sing it.
screen: `TALKING TO YOUR OWN SOUL` · `COUNTING THE BENEFITS` · `AS FAR AS EAST FROM WEST` · `HE KNOWS WE ARE DUST` · then, large: `FORGET NOT ALL HIS BENEFITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list three benefits you've received. Not big abstract ones. Specific. A meal someone cooked. A body that got you out of bed. A friend who texted back. A bill that got paid. Take your time and find three. Say each one quietly, the way the psalm does: who gave me this, who gave me that. Then sit with the list. If you pray, you can say the line: bless the Lord, O my soul. If you don't, let the three things sit there, remembered on purpose. The bell holds the time.
Bless the Lord. Psalm one hundred three's opening, spoken to the writer's own soul: a reminder to praise, and not to forget.
Your line: forget not all his benefits. Today, when a small kindness comes your way, stop for one breath and file it on purpose, the way you'd file a hurt. Day four hundred thirty-one.

432.title: The wild creation (Psalm 104)
432.hook: wine to gladden hearts, rocks for the badgers, a sea full of creatures
432.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians chant Psalm 104 at the opening of Vespers each evening, and many churches pray it at Pentecost and in services of thanksgiving for creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a soul told firmly not to forget. Your line was forget not all his benefits. Which small kindness did you file on purpose? Day four hundred thirty-two.

Lions roaring in the dark, asking for their dinner. Wild goats on cliffs too steep for anyone else. A stork nesting at the top of a fir tree. Donkeys drinking at a stream, birds singing in the branches above them. Then sunrise: the lions slink home to their dens, and a man heads out to work until evening. Out at sea, ships sail past an enormous creature that's simply playing in the waves. It sounds like the script for a nature documentary. It's a psalm, an ancient song of Israel. And it's one of the Bible's fullest looks at the natural world for its own sake. Today, Psalm one hundred four.
screen: `LIONS IN THE DARK.` → `GOATS ON THE CLIFFS.` → `A SEA CREATURE AT PLAY.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred four walks through creation roughly in the order of Genesis one: light, sky, waters, earth, plants, creatures, sun and moon. But where Genesis is spare, this psalm is crowded and noisy. Listen to verse eighteen in the King James Bible: "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies." Conies. The Hebrew is shaphan, almost certainly the rock hyrax: a small, furry, round animal that lives in rocky places across that land, and is, surprisingly, a distant cousin of the elephant. Some translations call it a badger. Whatever you call it, God made the rocks for it. Not for us. That's the striking thing about this psalm. Humans show up as one creature among many. People get wine "that maketh glad the heart of man," and oil, and bread. Fine. But the lions get their meat from God too, and the storks get the fir trees. Then the sea: "There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein." Leviathan, the sea monster that frightens readers elsewhere in the Bible, made here to play. And the center of the psalm: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all." Scholars have long noticed echoes of an older Egyptian hymn to the sun in this psalm; if so, the psalmist took that wonder and turned it toward the one God. Orthodox Christians open their evening service with this psalm, every night, and many churches read it at Pentecost, for verse thirty: thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created.
screen: `GENESIS ONE, CROWDED AND NOISY` · `ROCKS FOR THE CONIES` · `LEVIATHAN, MADE TO PLAY` · `IN WISDOM HAST THOU MADE THEM ALL` · then, large: `O LORD, HOW MANIFOLD ARE THY WORKS!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one wild creature. Look out a window, step outside, or call one to mind from the last few days. A pigeon, a spider in the corner, a squirrel, a gull, an ant on the counter. Watch it, or picture it, for the whole sit. How does it move? What is it looking for? Where will it sleep tonight? Don't name it as useful or a nuisance. Just let it be a creature with its own life. If you pray, you can say: in wisdom hast thou made them all. If you don't, simply watch. The bell holds the time.
The wild creation. Psalm one hundred four's crowded world: lions, goats, conies, storks and a playing leviathan, all fed by God.
Your line: all made in wisdom. Today, when a creature crosses your path, even one you'd usually shoo away, give it one second of attention as something made on purpose. Day four hundred thirty-two.

433.title: I lift up my eyes (Psalm 121)
433.hook: a pilgrim's song: my help comes from the Lord who made heaven and earth
433.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 121 before a journey, and it is often read at funerals and at services of blessing for travelers, pilgrims and people leaving home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, conies on the rocks and a leviathan made to play. Your line was all made in wisdom. Which creature got a second of your attention? Day four hundred thirty-three.

Three times a year, the law of Moses called the people up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. For many families that meant days on foot. Dusty roads, children on shoulders, old people on donkeys, everyone singing to keep the pace. And the city sits high in the hills, so the last stretch is always uphill. Fifteen psalms in a row, one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty-four, carry the same heading in the King James Bible: A Song of degrees. Songs of going up. Many think pilgrims sang them on that road. Today, the most beloved of them, sung by someone looking up at the hills ahead.
screen: `THREE FEASTS A YEAR.` → `THE ROAD GOES UPHILL.` → `SONGS OF GOING UP.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred twenty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." It reads like a statement: my help comes from the hills. But the Hebrew can just as easily be read as a question, and many translations print it that way: I lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from? Why ask? The hills could be lovely, or they could be frightening. Bandits hid in them. Some readers think of hilltop shrines to other gods, offering help of their own. Either way, the pilgrim looks up, and the next line answers: "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." Not from the hills. From the one who made them. Then the voice changes. Someone else seems to answer the pilgrim, maybe a friend on the road, maybe a priest: "He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber." Suffer means allow. Your foot won't slip on the path. "Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." Here's a detail you can't hear in English. In just eight verses, the Hebrew word for keep, shamar, appears six times. Keep, keep, keep. The one who keeps watches your coming and going, by day and by night. And the last verse: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." Every door you walk through, out and back. Christians have long prayed this psalm before a journey.
screen: `A STATEMENT, OR A QUESTION?` · `NOT FROM THE HILLS` · `HE NEITHER SLUMBERS NOR SLEEPS` · `KEEP, SIX TIMES IN EIGHT VERSES` · then, large: `MY HELP COMETH FROM THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look toward the hills, or the horizon. If you can see far, a skyline, a ridge, the edge of a field, the top of the tallest building nearby, turn toward it now. If you can't, close your eyes and picture the farthest place you've ever looked out over. Lift your eyes slowly, the way the pilgrim did. Let your breathing slow. Ask the pilgrim's question quietly: where does my help come from? If you pray, you can answer with the psalm: my help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth. If you don't, just keep looking, and let the distance do its work. The bell holds the time.
I lift up my eyes. The opening of Psalm one hundred twenty-one, a pilgrim's song looking up at the hills and asking where help comes from.
screen: `I LIFT UP MY EYES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: my help comes. Today, every time you walk out a door, and every time you come back in, remember the last verse: your going out and your coming in. Day four hundred thirty-three.

434.title: Like those who dream (Psalm 126)
434.hook: those who sow in tears shall reap in joy
434.carry: sow in tears, reap in joy
434.howItsDone: Christians often pray Psalm 126 in times of waiting and loss, and its sowing verse is sung in hymns such as "Bringing in the Sheaves"; Jewish families sing it before the grace after meals on Sabbaths and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pilgrim looking up at the hills. Your line was my help comes. Did verse eight walk out the door with you? Day four hundred thirty-four.

The phone rings. The scan came back clear. Or: the visa was approved. Or: they found him, he's safe. And for a few seconds you can't take it in. You laugh in a way that's half crying. You ask them to say it again. You actually pinch your arm, because news this good feels like the kind of thing you wake up from. Psalm one hundred twenty-six begins in exactly that moment, for a whole people. Something they had stopped expecting has happened, and the only word for it is a dream. Today, the psalm of the dreamers, and the farmer who weeps while planting.
screen: `THE SCAN CAME BACK CLEAR.` → `SAY IT AGAIN.` → `IT FEELS LIKE A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Another song of going up, from the pilgrims' collection. In the King James Bible: "When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream. Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing." Many readers hear the return from exile in Babylon here, when the Persian king Cyrus let the deported families go home. Some scholars translate the Hebrew more broadly, as when the Lord restored the fortunes of Zion. Either way, the dreamers aren't asleep. They're wide awake, and it's too good to believe. Even the neighboring nations say: the Lord has done great things for them. Then, in verse four, the mood shifts. "Turn again our captivity, O LORD, as the streams in the south." The south is the Negev, desert country. Its stream beds sit dry most of the year, and then, after a heavy rain, they fill with rushing water almost overnight. So the people are asking for it again. The first homecoming wasn't the end of the hard part. Then the line everyone remembers: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him." Why would a farmer weep while sowing? Some readers picture a hungry year, when every handful of seed thrown into the ground is a handful you can't eat. Planting is an act of hope that costs something now. The psalm doesn't skip the tears. It promises they won't be the last word in the field. A nineteenth-century hymn, Bringing in the Sheaves, grew from this verse.
screen: `AWAKE, BUT IT FEELS LIKE A DREAM` · `STREAMS IN THE DRY SOUTH` · `SEED YOU COULD HAVE EATEN` · `SOW IN TEARS, BRING THE SHEAVES` · then, large: `THEY THAT SOW IN TEARS SHALL REAP IN JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant something, even a thought. If you have a seed and a pot, wonderful. If not, plant something you can't see yet. Think of a hard place in your life, the dry stream bed. Now choose one small seed to put into it. A kind word you'll say to someone. A first step on something you've been putting off. A hope you've been too tired to name. Hold it for the sit, the way a farmer holds seed before throwing it. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, just plant it on purpose. The bell holds the time.
Like those who dream. Psalm one hundred twenty-six: a people restored, laughing like dreamers, still sowing in tears.

Your line: sow in tears, reap in joy. That was this week in the Psalms: numbering our days, under his wings, a new song, bless the Lord, the wild creation, lifting our eyes, and the dreamers. Today, do one small hopeful thing that costs you a little now. Day four hundred thirty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise that sad times always end happily.
what it means: a people already restored, still asking for more, and a farmer who plants through tears.
